UPC

ArithmeticDivisibilityNumber Theory
Game: A shop product code has twelve digits, and the last one is worked out from the others; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Press the left or right half of one of the first eleven digits to add one or take one away, or select a digit and type a new one. Watch the last digit and the bars change.

Look for the math

The UPC-A code on a shop item is twelve digits. The last is a check digit: it is chosen so that a little sum comes out a multiple of ten. That way a scanner can notice a digit that was read or typed wrongly.

The rule for the last digit

Write the digits d1 d2 … d12, with d12 last. The applet and its page use

3d1 + d2 + 3d3 + d4 + … + 3d11 + d12 = 0 (mod 10)

The weights 3 and 1 alternate. Calling the sums of the digits in the odd and even places S_odd and S_even, this is the same as 3 S_odd + S_even = 0 (mod 10). The applet fills in d12 = (10 − (3 S_odd + S_even mod 10)) mod 10. The logic test compared this with a second transcription of the applet's own FixCheckDigit on 330,000 prefixes — every digit value in every one of the eleven places — and all 330,000 finished codes satisfied the page's formula.

What the check catches

In modular arithmetic, changing one of the first eleven digits by c changes the sum by 3c or c. Neither can be a multiple of ten unless c is, so one wrong digit is always caught: the test tried every wrong value in every place of 1,000 codes. Swapping two neighbours a, b changes the sum by ±2(a − b); that can be a multiple of ten when the two digits differ by 5, so that one slip can go unnoticed. The check digit is the only digit 0–9 that makes the sum work, which the test confirmed on 1,000 prefixes.

The bars

The code is 95 modules wide: a 101 guard at each end and 01010 in the middle, seven modules for each digit. The left six digits use the odd patterns and the right six the colour-inverse patterns, so a reader can tell which way up the code is. The test decoded the bars of 100,000 random codes back into the right twelve digits. Put a 0 in front of a UPC-A code and you have an EAN-13 with the same check digit and the same bars.

Try swapping two neighbouring digits that differ by 5: the bars change, but the last digit does not. Can you find another pair the check digit misses?
